_meta.keyKnowledge: We are learning about the factors that influence the decisions we make as consumers and with our money.

toLevel2.question: Advertising is designed to influence what people want to buy or try.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Advertising sets out to shape consumer wants and persuade people to choose certain products.

distractors.explanation: Advertising clearly aims to influence buyer choices, which is why companies pay for it.

toLevel2.question: Peer pressure has no effect on the buying choices young people make at any time.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Peer pressure can shape what young people buy, including snacks, clothing, and tech.

distractors.explanation: Treating peer influence as zero ignores how strongly friends shape spending choices.

toLevel2.question: Needs are things a person must have to live well, such as food, water, and shelter.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Food, water, shelter, and basic clothing are widely classed as needs because life requires them.

distractors.explanation: Needs are commonly defined as essentials for living, so this statement is correct.

toLevel2.question: A want is something a person would like to have but does not need to live.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Wants describe non-essential items people would enjoy, like a new game or extra snack.

distractors.explanation: This is the standard definition of a want in consumer education at this level.

toLevel2.question: Price is never a factor when a person decides whether to buy a product or service.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Price is one of the main factors most consumers weigh before buying anything.

distractors.explanation: Treating price as irrelevant ignores how budgets and value shape every consumer choice.

toLevel2.question: Brand recognition can influence which product a shopper picks off a crowded shelf.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Familiar brand names often pull shopper attention and shape choices on busy shelves.

distractors.explanation: Brand recognition is a well-known factor in how consumers pick between similar products.

toLevel2.question: Quality has no link to whether a product is worth the price a customer pays.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Higher quality can justify a higher price; low quality reduces the value buyers receive.

distractors.explanation: Treating quality as separate from value misses a core idea in consumer choice.

toLevel2.question: Friends have no influence on the consumer choices a young person makes in any setting.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Friends shape many consumer choices, from what to wear to which apps to use.

distractors.explanation: Treating friend influence as zero ignores everyday peer effects on spending.

toLevel2.question: Every advertisement only ever shows facts and never tries to persuade the viewer at all.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Most advertising mixes information with persuasion techniques designed to shape choices.

distractors.explanation: Treating ads as fact-only ignores the persuasion techniques companies pay to use.

toLevel2.question: Smart consumers think about price, quality, and real need before they decide to buy something.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Comparing price, quality, and real need is a core habit of careful consumer choice.

distractors.explanation: These three factors are commonly taught as the basis of thoughtful consumer choice.

toLevel2.question: Wanting something and needing something always mean exactly the same thing to a consumer.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Wants and needs differ: needs are essentials for living; wants are extras a person would enjoy.

distractors.explanation: Treating wants and needs as identical misses a basic distinction in consumer education.

toLevel2.question: Young consumers can never tell the difference between persuasion and real information online.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: With practice, young consumers learn to spot persuasion techniques and check real information.

distractors.explanation: Treating young people as unable to tell the difference underestimates skills they can build.

toLevel2.question: What does advertising try to do to consumers?
toLevel2.correct: Influence consumer wants and shape what people choose to buy
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Advertising aims to influence wants and shape what consumers choose.

distractors.answer: Stop every consumer from buying anything in any local shop
distractors.explanation: Advertisers want to encourage buying, not stop people from buying anything.

distractors.answer: Hide all product information from buyers in every market in
distractors.explanation: Most ads share information about a product, even while trying to persuade.

toLevel2.correctExplanation: Peer pressure is the influence friends and classmates have on what a person buys.

distractors.answer: Pressure from a parent to save money rather than spend it on snacks
distractors.explanation: Pressure from a parent is family influence, not peer pressure between friends.

distractors.answer: A rule from a school that bans every student from buying any item
distractors.explanation: A school rule is a regulation, not the peer-to-peer influence between friends.

toLevel2.question: Which item is best classified as a need rather than a want?

toLevel2.correctExplanation: Drinking water is essential for living, so it is classed as a need.

distractors.answer: A new computer game released by a popular online company in
distractors.explanation: A new computer game is a non-essential extra, so it is a want.

distractors.answer: A pair of designer headphones promoted by a famous influencer in

toLevel2.correctExplanation: A latest-model smart watch is a non-essential item, which makes it a want.

distractors.explanation: Drinking water is essential for living, so it is a need rather than a want.

distractors.answer: Healthy food on the dinner table for every member of the family
distractors.explanation: Healthy food is essential for living, so it is a need rather than a want.

toLevel2.question: Why does price matter to most consumers when they choose what to buy?

distractors.answer: Price has no effect on any consumer choice in any shop at any time

distractors.answer: Price is set by the buyer alone after every product reaches the shelf in
distractors.explanation: Price is set by sellers, not by individual buyers after stocking the shelf.

distractors.explanation: The day of the week has no link to product quality.

distractors.answer: A buyer reading a story about a singer in a magazine while waiting in a long queue

toLevel2.question: Which one of these best describes a smart consumer choice?
toLevel2.correct: Comparing price, quality, and real need before deciding what to buy at the shop in
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Comparing price, quality, and real need is the basis of a smart consumer choice.

distractors.answer: Buying every product an advertisement shows on a screen without any thought in maths and

distractors.answer: A child counting the cars passing the school gate during a maths lesson on Tuesday in maths and

toLevel2.correct: What friends or classmates wear and consider fashionable at school in maths and

distractors.answer: The price tag at a store on a single Tuesday afternoon in winter

distractors.answer: The number of birds visiting a garden during a long weekend in spring
distractors.explanation: Birds in a garden have no link to a young person's clothing choice.

toLevel2.question: Which list includes only factors that influence a consumer choice?

toLevel2.correctExplanation: Price, quality, brand, advertising, and peer influence are all consumer-choice factors.

distractors.answer: Trees, rivers, mountains, oceans, and clouds visible from a regional airport in

toLevel3.question: A child who copies a friend in choosing a snack at a stall is showing peer pressure at work.
toLevel3.correct: True
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Copying a friend's snack choice is a clear example of peer pressure shaping a buying decision.

distractors.explanation: Copying a friend's choice is a textbook example of how peer pressure influences a buyer.

toLevel3.question: Advertising slots during a popular children's show only target young viewers by accident.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Companies choose those slots on purpose to reach young viewers; the targeting is planned.

distractors.explanation: Treating the targeting as accidental ignores how carefully companies pick advertising slots.

toLevel3.question: Two products at the same price can still differ in quality and in the value they offer a buyer.
toLevel3.correct: True
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Products at the same price can vary in materials, durability, or features that affect value.

distractors.explanation: Same-price products often differ in quality, which is why careful comparison matters.

toLevel3.question: A higher price on a product always means it is better quality than every cheaper option.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Price does not guarantee quality; some cheaper products match or beat pricier ones.

distractors.explanation: Treating price as a guarantee of quality ignores tests that show cheaper goods can match dearer ones.

toLevel3.question: Recognising the techniques used in an ad can help a person resist its influence on choices.
toLevel3.correct: True
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Spotting techniques such as bright colours or celebrity faces helps buyers think before buying.

distractors.explanation: Awareness of advertising techniques is a recognised tool for stronger consumer choice.

toLevel3.question: Brand loyalty has no effect on what a regular shopper buys week after week at the shops.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Brand loyalty leads many shoppers to choose the same brand again and again from habit and trust.

distractors.explanation: Treating loyalty as inactive ignores how often shoppers stick to brands they already trust.

toLevel3.question: Classifying an item as a need or a want has no effect on a consumer spending choice at all.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Sorting items into needs and wants helps people set priorities and avoid regret about choices.

distractors.explanation: Treating the need-want sort as useless ignores its core role in budgeting and spending choices.

toLevel3.question: Paid posts by online influencers do not count as advertising in any setting at any time.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Paid influencer posts are a form of advertising, even when they look like personal recommendations.

distractors.explanation: Treating paid posts as not-advertising misses one of the main forms of online persuasion today.
